title: The Frisbee and the pie tins
hook: The Frisbee is named after a bakery whose pie tins students tossed around.
peek: Long before plastic flying discs, college students in New England threw empty metal tins from the Frisbie Pie Company of Connecticut. When the toy firm Wham-O heard about the campus craze, it renamed its plastic disc after the bakery, with a slightly different spelling.
lede: The Frisbie Pie Company of Bridgeport, Connecticut, baked pies from the 1870s until the 1950s and sold many of them near colleges. The story goes that students at Yale and other campuses tossed the empty tins, embossed with the Frisbie name, across lawns. When a plastic flying disc later went on sale, it ended up named after the bakery.

bullets.text: In 1948 Fred Morrison, a Californian who had tossed cake pans on the beach with his future wife, made a plastic disc with Warren Franscioni. He later refined it into the Pluto Platter, sold with a flying saucer theme.

The toy company Wham-O bought the rights to Morrison's disc in 1957. Its founders heard that students in the East called throwing a disc frisbie-ing, and in 1958 they renamed the toy Frisbee, changing the spelling.
The bakery was founded by William Russell Frisbie and grew into a sizeable business serving New England. It closed in 1958, the same year its name went onto a plastic toy.

In the 1960s Wham-O designer Ed Headrick reshaped the disc with ridges on top and a heavier rim, so it flew straighter and farther. His changes turned a novelty into a sports disc, and he went on to help found disc golf.
